teaser: A woman in white, in front of white, rejected twice before anyone understood why.
review_notes:
Malevich's White on White dated 1918 (MoMA): check.
NGA describes the rug as a wolf skin; some sources say bear.
Whistler's illness after the painting attributed to lead white poisoning: commonly stated, not certain.
Dimensions about 213 x 108 cm: check.
The Paris critic who called it a 'symphony in white' was Paul Mantz (1863); Whistler adopted the musical title some years later.
Hiffernan raising Whistler's son Charles Hanson (born 1870): check.

lesson.text: In 1918 the Russian painter Kazimir Malevich hung a white square on a white ground and called it finished. It is often described as the moment painting let go of the visible world. Fifty-six years earlier, a 27-year-old American in Paris had already asked a quieter version of the same question: how much of a picture can you build from white alone?

His answer stands over two meters tall, about 213 by 108 centimeters (7 feet by 3 and a half). A young woman in a white dress stands before a white curtain. Her face gives nothing away. James McNeill Whistler worked on it through the winter of 1861 to 1862, in a studio he had draped in white cloth.

The model was Joanna Hiffernan, an Irishwoman with copper hair who was his companion and, for about six years, the face of his best pictures. She stood for him day after day, in winter light, while he fussed over tones most people would call identical.
They are not identical. Before the picture opens, guess how many different whites it holds. Then compare the curtain, the dress and the cuff, one after the other.

lesson.title: Three whites
lesson.text: White against white. Each stop is the same color on paper, and a different one in paint.

spots.title: The curtain
spots.text: A cool, slightly gray white, with a woven pattern of small flowers picked out in thicker paint. The folds are drawn with long vertical strokes.

spots.title: The dress
spots.text: Warmer and creamier. The tucked bodice and the puffed, pleated sleeve are built from short dabs, so the fabric looks crisp where the curtain looks soft.

spots.title: Cuff and lily
spots.text: The brightest white in the picture is the stiff cuff. Under it, her hand hangs loose and holds a single white flower, a lily, pointing at the floor.

lesson.text: Whistler separated the whites by temperature (cooler or warmer) and by texture, not by outline. That is a painter's problem set for its own sake, and in 1862 it was a strange thing to offer the public, who expected a picture to tell them who this woman was and what had happened to her.

The main pigment here is lead white, which is poisonous. Whistler fell ill after months of work on the picture and went to the coast to recover. Lead poisoning from his own paint is the usual explanation.

London's Royal Academy refused the painting in 1862. A small gallery showed it instead under the title “The Woman in White”, the name of a bestselling mystery novel. Whistler protested in print: his picture, he wrote, simply showed a girl dressed in white standing in front of a white curtain.

Then Paris refused it too. In 1863 the official Salon rejected so many works that the emperor allowed a separate show for the losers, the Salon des Refusés. Whistler's girl hung there, in the same exhibition as Manet's “Luncheon on the Grass”, and drew crowds, jokes and a few serious admirers.

Viewers wanted a story so badly that they invented them: a bride the morning after, a ghost, a sleepwalker. The picture does offer one clue that is anything but calm. It is on the floor, and it is looking at you.
There is a second face in this painting, with its teeth showing. Where?

spots.title: The animal
spots.text: Her feet rest on an animal skin, and its head lies in the foreground with open jaws. Loose, quick strokes make the fur. It is the only expressive face in the picture, and the only threat.

lesson.text: A snarling head under a motionless girl: Whistler never explained it. What is certain is how differently the bottom of the canvas is painted. Up top everything is hushed and vertical. Down here the brush gets rough, the colors arrive, and the floor tilts toward you.

Whistler later renamed the picture “Symphony in White, No. 1”, after a French critic compared it to music. The title tells you how to look: at an arrangement of tones, the way you would listen to a piece with no words.
A critic complained that a later “Symphony in White” also contained yellow, brown and flesh color. Whistler's reply: does a symphony in F contain no other note than F, F, F?

spots.title: Her face
spots.text: Pale skin, red lips, eyes that look past you. The dark red hair is the strongest color in the upper canvas and frames the face like a hood.

spots.title: Signature
spots.text: “Whistler 1862”, written in blue-gray across the top of the curtain. He would later replace his name with a small butterfly emblem.

spots.title: Dropped flowers
spots.text: White and purple blossoms lie scattered on the fur at her feet, as if they had slipped from her hand.

spots.title: The carpet
spots.text: Blue patterns in choppy little strokes. After so much white, this patch of blue reads as loud as a shout.

spots.title: The hem
spots.text: The skirt spreads across the fur in a wide, flat shape. Its edge is where the white world above meets the colored world below.

lesson.text: Joanna Hiffernan did more than pose. She kept Whistler's accounts, sold his work when he was away, and later helped raise a son he had with another woman.
Whistler and Hiffernan eventually went separate ways, and the painting crossed the Atlantic. It now hangs in the National Gallery of Art in Washington, still declining to say what it is about.

quiz.question: Who posed for the painting?
quiz.explanation: Hiffernan was Whistler's companion and main model at the time.

quiz.question: Where was the painting shown in Paris in 1863?
quiz.explanation: The Salon rejected it, so it hung in the exhibition of refused works.

quiz.question: How does Whistler tell his whites apart?
quiz.explanation: The curtain is cooler and softer, the dress warmer and crisper.

quiz.question: What lies under the woman's feet?
options: An animal skin with its head
quiz.explanation: She stands on a fur rug whose snarling head faces the viewer.

quiz.question: Why did Whistler add “Symphony” to the title?
options: To present the picture as an arrangement of tones, like music
Because it was painted in a concert hall
Because the model was a singer
quiz.explanation: A critic's musical comparison gave him the idea, and he adopted it.

facts.text: Whistler said the painting illustrated the novel “The Woman in White”.
facts.explanation: He denied it and said it simply showed a girl in white before a white curtain.

facts.text: The painting was rejected in both London and Paris.
facts.explanation: The Royal Academy refused it in 1862 and the Paris Salon in 1863.

facts.text: The picture contains no color other than white.
facts.explanation: Her red hair, the blue carpet and the flowers all break the white.
